acetaminophen.tagline: The basic painkiller and fever reducer, easiest on the stomach
acetaminophen.lead: This is the most basic medicine for pain and fever. It doesn't calm inflammation, but it's easier on the stomach, kidneys and heart than anti-inflammatory painkillers, so clinics lay it down first as the **base** of pain treatment. The thing to watch most is **the daily total**. If you add up the acetaminophen hidden in cold medicines and combination painkillers and go over 4 g a day, the liver gets damaged. If you drink more than three drinks every day or have liver problems, talk to a doctor or pharmacist first (leaflet).
sideEffects: Side effects are rare at normal doses
stop: Nausea and vomiting with pain in the upper right tummy, or yellowing of the eyes or skin (signs of liver damage)
A rash that spreads or blisters
tips: One of the few painkillers you can take on an empty stomach. With a glass of water.

Don't double the dose because it 'feels weak'. Taking it **at the same time as ibuprofen, a different type, isn't recommended in principle** (leaflet, UK guidance), but clinics sometimes use the two together or alternately if one isn't enough — keep each medicine's own interval and daily total. If you're pregnant, have a stomach ulcer or kidney disease, or take blood thinners, you may need to avoid ibuprofen.
Don't split or chew extended-release (8-hour) tablets.
If fever lasts more than 3 days or pain more than 10 days, don't increase the medicine — see a doctor.

faq.q: Is Tylenol the ingredient name?
faq.a: No — Tylenol is a brand name, and the ingredient is **acetaminophen**. Several other Korean brands contain the same ingredient, and many cold medicines and combination painkillers also contain 300–650 mg each. The ingredient list on the back of the box shows straight away whether they overlap.

faq.q: If the fever goes down, am I better?
faq.a: No. A fever reducer lowers fever for a while — it controls the symptom, it doesn't treat the cause. If fever lasts more than 3 days, goes down and comes back, or you feel very unwell, have the cause checked.

faq.q: Is three times a day OK?
faq.a: Yes. 1–2 tablets of 500 mg 30 minutes after breakfast, lunch and dinner, at least 4 hours apart. Even if you take extra when it hurts, don't go over 8 tablets (4 g) a day.

faq.q: I have a stomach ulcer — is it easier on the stomach than anti-inflammatories?
faq.a: In an overseas study (UK, 2001), under 2 g a day it didn't raise the risk of stomach bleeding and was easier on the stomach than anti-inflammatories, but above 2 g a day the risk of stomach bleeding rose 3.6 times. Korean leaflets say not to take it if you have an ulcer now, so talk to a doctor or pharmacist first.

acetaminophen.children: **500 mg tablets are from age 12** (Korean approval). For younger children, give **children's suspension or syrup** by body weight — don't split adult tablets for them. Syrup is from 4 months; under age 2, talk to a doctor.

ibuprofen.tagline: Among pharmacy anti-inflammatories, one of the easiest on the stomach
ibuprofen.lead: An anti-inflammatory painkiller that reduces pain by calming inflammation. Among the anti-inflammatories you can buy at a pharmacy, it's **one of the easiest on the stomach at low doses (up to 1,200 mg a day)**, and it works fast. It works better than acetaminophen for muscle and joint pain, period pain and toothache.
sideEffects: Swelling, higher blood pressure (high doses, long use)
stop: Black stools or vomiting blood (stomach bleeding)
Breathlessness, wheezing or a swelling face (allergic reaction)
Passing much less urine or swollen ankles

If a rash spreads over the body with fever, or there are blisters, peeling skin, sores in the mouth and eyes, or a swollen face with lumps in the neck, **stop at once and go to the emergency department** (severe skin reaction — usually within a month of starting)
If an allergy such as hives or face swelling comes with **chest tightness or chest pain, call 119 at once** (Kounis syndrome, where allergy tightens the heart's blood vessels)
tips: Right after a meal, or with milk or a snack. An empty stomach increases heartburn.
Hitting the pain firmly with 400 mg early and then continuing with 200–400 mg works better than taking little bits.

**If you're 65 or older, or take blood thinners or steroids,** keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use anti-inflammatories — if you've had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid suppressant at a clinic is surer. Others can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if it keeps burning.
With a glass of water. When you're dehydrated, the kidneys struggle.

faq.q: Are the different ibuprofen brands different medicines?
faq.a: Most contain the same ingredient, ibuprofen (some contain dexibuprofen). Even if the brand names differ, taking two with the same ingredient together is doubling up (strength and form can differ by product — if unsure, check with a pharmacist).

faq.q: Can I take it with acetaminophen?
faq.a: In principle taking them at the same time isn't recommended (leaflet, UK guidance), but clinics sometimes use them together or alternately when fever or pain isn't controlled. Together they work better than either alone — keep each medicine's own interval and daily total. But don't double up on two anti-inflammatories, such as ibuprofen + naproxen.

ibuprofen.children: From 6 months. Avoid during dehydration (vomiting, diarrhoea), when the strain on the kidneys is greater.

famotidine.tagline: The strongest acid suppressant you can buy at a pharmacy — only 10 mg is non-prescription
famotidine.lead: An H2 blocker that reduces stomach acid production. In Korea, strong acid suppressants such as omeprazole are prescription-only, so **the strongest acid suppressant you can buy at a pharmacy is famotidine 10 mg**. It's a medicine you can try first from the pharmacy when your stomach burns while taking anti-inflammatories or you're worried about the strain on your stomach (it's weaker than prescription acid suppressants). But it's **a medicine that reduces heartburn** — at this dose it hasn't been shown to prevent stomach bleeding or ulcers from anti-inflammatories; those studies used prescription doses (40–80 mg a day). It works later than antacids (30 minutes–1 hour) but lasts 10–12 hours. **Only 10 mg products are sold at pharmacies; 20 mg and above need a prescription.**
stop: Black stools, vomiting blood
Difficulty swallowing
tips: When buying it with an anti-inflammatory, just ask for “famotidine 10 mg”.
If heartburn is bad right now, an antacid first; famotidine for prevention and keeping it at bay.
If you need it for more than 14 days, don't increase it — see a doctor. If Helicobacter bacteria are the cause, there's separate treatment to get rid of them.

faq.q: Why buy it with an anti-inflammatory?
faq.a:
Anti-inflammatories also reduce the substances that protect the stomach lining, so they can cause heartburn and ulcers. Famotidine is the strongest acid suppressant you can buy at a pharmacy, so if you're 65 or older or take blood thinners or steroids, try taking it alongside **to ease heartburn** (up to 20 mg a day). If your stomach keeps burning or doesn't improve, see a doctor.

But it hasn't been shown that pharmacy doses prevent ulcers or bleeding from anti-inflammatories. The trial where famotidine reduced stomach ulcers used a prescription dose (80 mg a day), and at 40 mg a day the difference in ulcers wasn't clear. If you've had a stomach ulcer or need to take it long term, get a prescription acid suppressant from a clinic.

faq.q: How much less if my kidneys are poor?
faq.a: The dose is set by your doctor. For reference, the US label reduces it, even on prescription, to 20 mg every other day if the kidney function test (creatinine clearance) is under 30 mL per minute — half of taking pharmacy 10 mg twice a day.

naproxen.tagline: Long-lasting, and the anti-inflammatory least likely to raise heart attack and stroke risk — but harder on the stomach
naproxen.lead: A long-acting anti-inflammatory painkiller — one dose lasts 8–12 hours. In a 2013 pooled analysis of anti-inflammatory trials worldwide, it was **the only anti-inflammatory painkiller that didn't increase heart and blood vessel events**, so clinics often choose it for pain in people with high blood pressure or heart disease. But **naproxen, like other anti-inflammatories, roughly doubles the risk of heart failure (a weak heart causing swelling and breathlessness).** If you have heart failure or severe high blood pressure, don't take it — talk to a doctor. On the other hand, **its strain on the stomach is about twice that of ibuprofen**. For period pain, a loading dose of '2 capsules for the first dose' is approved.
sideEffects: Heartburn, indigestion (more common than with ibuprofen)
stop: Black stools, vomiting blood
Breathlessness or a swelling face
Passing less urine, swollen ankles

If a rash spreads over the body with fever, or there are blisters, peeling skin, sores in the mouth and eyes, or a swollen face with lumps in the neck, **stop at once and go to the emergency department** (severe skin reaction — usually within a month of starting)
tips: For period pain, hit it firmly with 2 capsules as the first dose as soon as it starts (or the day before), then 1 capsule every 6–8 hours regularly for 2–3 days.

Always after food. **If you're 65 or older, or take blood thinners or steroids,** keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use anti-inflammatories — if you've had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid suppressant at a clinic is surer. Others can add it only when the stomach burns, and see a doctor if it keeps burning.
Don't go over 1,250 mg (5 capsules) a day.

faq.q: I have heart disease — what if I need an anti-inflammatory?
faq.a: In the 2013 pooled analysis it was the only anti-inflammatory painkiller that didn't increase heart and blood vessel events, so clinics often choose it. But naproxen, like other anti-inflammatories, roughly doubles the risk of heart failure (a weak heart causing swelling and breathlessness). If you have heart failure or severe high blood pressure, don't take it — talk to a doctor. Its strain on the stomach is about twice that of ibuprofen, so always take it after food, and if you're 65 or older or take blood thinners or steroids, keep pharmacy famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside.

faq.q: How do I take it for period pain?
faq.a: As soon as it starts (or the day before), hit it firmly with 2 capsules as the first dose, then 1 capsule every 6–8 hours regularly for 2–3 days. Don't go over 5 capsules (1,250 mg) a day.

naproxen.children: Check each product's age limit. Some products can be used by teenagers (12 and over) with period pain.

trimebutine.tagline: Relaxes squeezing pain — the gentler choice for older people
trimebutine.lead: A medicine that calms hollow organs such as the gut or bladder when they **squeeze out of control**. What's unusual is that it doesn't push only one way — if they're moving too much it slows them, and if they're sluggish it speeds them up. So it can be used for both the diarrhoea and the constipation type. **It has no anticholinergic action**, so there's almost no dry mouth, glare or blocked urine, which makes it easier than butylscopolamine for older people. **It's sold at pharmacies.**
stop: If your skin turns yellow or urine gets dark, stop and see a doctor
If a rash or hives appear, stop
tips: It works best **30 minutes before a meal**.
A warm hot-water bottle on the sore spot helps the spasm settle faster along with the medicine.
If you're taking it for bladder pain, **drinking enough water and not holding in urine** matters as much as the medicine.

faq.q: Can I take this for cystitis?
faq.a:
Cystitis pain is spasm pain from **the bladder squeezing**, so adding an antispasmodic makes it much more comfortable. Clinics sometimes use tiropramide, and trimebutine can also help. But **this medicine doesn't kill bacteria** — cystitis is treated with prescription antibiotics, and holding out for days on painkillers and antispasmodics alone can let it reach the kidneys. Think of it as **a medicine to add while you're being treated**.

(Using it for bladder spasm isn't confirmed by large trials — it's **based on how it works and clinical experience**.)

faq.q: How is it different from butylscopolamine?
faq.a: Butylscopolamine is **an anticholinergic**, so it works well but can cause dry mouth, glare and difficulty passing urine. **If you have glaucoma or an enlarged prostate, avoid it altogether.** Trimebutine doesn't have that action, so it's easier on older people. On the other hand, butylscopolamine starts working a little faster.

trimebutine.children: For children, the dose is adjusted by weight using syrup. Talk to a paediatrician.

cetirizine.tagline: Once-a-day second-generation antihistamine — among the drowsier of its group, so take it at bedtime
cetirizine.lead: A second-generation antihistamine that works for 24 hours on one tablet a day for allergic rhinitis, hives and itching. It's the drowsiest of the second-generation group (3.5 times more drowsiness than loratadine in a large observational study), so the standard is to take it before bed.
stop: If you're too drowsy to work during the day, switch to another ingredient
If hives last more than 6 weeks, see a doctor
If your face or lips swell or you get breathless, go to the emergency department at once
tips: Taking it in the evening and sleeping reduces daytime drowsiness.
If your rhinitis is mainly a 'blocked nose', antihistamines alone aren't enough — a steroid nasal spray (prescription) is the first-line treatment.

faq.q: Will it make me drowsy if I take it during the day?
faq.a: It's the drowsiest of the second-generation group (3.5 times that of loratadine), so the standard is to take it before bed. Before driving or precise work, loratadine or fexofenadine is safer.

faq.q: Doesn't it work for a blocked nose?
faq.a: Antihistamines alone aren't enough. For rhinitis that's mainly a blocked nose, a steroid nasal spray (prescription) is the first-line treatment.

cetirizine.children: Tablets from age 6; syrup for younger children.

loratadine.tagline: Once a day with hardly any drowsiness — for daytime
loratadine.lead: A second-generation antihistamine that causes hardly any drowsiness (it was the baseline drug for drowsiness risk in a large cohort study). It starts working a little more slowly than cetirizine, but one tablet a day lasts 24 hours, and you can use it while driving or working.
stop: If hives last more than 6 weeks, see a doctor
If your face or lips swell or you get breathless, go to the emergency department at once
If drowsiness is bad, switch to another ingredient
tips: An antihistamine you can take in the morning.
If it feels too weak, switch to cetirizine (at bedtime).

faq.q: Can I take it in the morning?
faq.a: Yes. It causes hardly any drowsiness, so it's for daytime. If it feels too weak, switch to cetirizine (at bedtime).

faq.q: What if my liver isn't good?
faq.a: If liver function is reduced, it's taken every other day. Tell the pharmacist.

loratadine.children: **Tablets from age 6, syrup from age 2** (approved ages differ by form).

dexibuprofen.tagline: The 'active half' of ibuprofen — the same effect from a smaller amount
dexibuprofen.lead: Ibuprofen is a 50:50 mix of two mirror-image molecules, and dexibuprofen is just the one that actually relieves pain. So **300 mg has about the same effect as ibuprofen 400 mg**, and in crossover trials it started working a little sooner. Claims of 'fewer' stomach side effects are an assumption based on the total amount being half — there isn't yet enough independent comparative evidence.
stop: Black stools, vomiting blood
Breathlessness or a swelling face
Passing less urine

If a rash spreads over the body with fever, or there are blisters, peeling skin, sores in the mouth and eyes, or a swollen face with lumps in the neck, **stop at once and go to the emergency department** (severe skin reaction — usually within a month of starting)
If an allergy such as hives or face swelling comes with **chest tightness or chest pain, call 119 at once** (Kounis syndrome, where allergy tightens the heart's blood vessels)
tips: With food.
Brand names that sound stronger can make it seem like a stronger medicine, but it's in the same class as ibuprofen 400 mg.

faq.q: Is dexibuprofen 300 mg stronger than ibuprofen 400 mg?
faq.a: No, it's the same class. It's just the part of ibuprofen that actually relieves pain, so 300 mg has about the same effect as ibuprofen 400 mg. Brand names that sound stronger make it easy to mistake it for a stronger medicine.

faq.q: Is it gentler on the stomach?
faq.a: That's an assumption based on the total amount being half — there isn't yet enough independent comparative evidence. Take it with food, and don't double up with other anti-inflammatory painkillers.

diclofenac-topical.tagline: An anti-inflammatory you rub on for sprains and bruises — in trials, about 3 in 5 people who used it benefited
diclofenac-topical.lead: In an analysis pooling studies of fresh sprains and bruises, **diclofenac gel came out best in 2 trials (about 3 in 5 people who used it benefited).** But there's little data comparing topical medicines directly with each other. Side effects at the application site were similar to placebo. It was also shown to work for knee arthritis over 6–12 weeks. Unlike oral diclofenac, there's hardly any worry about the heart or stomach.
stop: Stop if the area turns red and itchy
If it's no better after a week, see a doctor
Stop if your stomach burns while using it together with an oral anti-inflammatory
tips: Rub it in until absorbed and wash your hands.
For a sprained ankle or wrist pain, this gel + a cold pack is clinics' first choice before tablets.

faq.q: I've sprained my ankle — is it better than tablets?
faq.a: About the same. In an analysis pooling several studies, topical anti-inflammatories seemed to reduce pain about as well as oral ones, and with diclofenac gel about 3 in 5 people benefited in 2 trials. Side effects at the application site were similar to placebo. This gel + a cold pack is clinics' first choice.

faq.q: How much do I apply?
faq.a: Rub in an amount the size of 1–2 cherries 3–4 times a day and wash your hands. Don't apply it to wounds or mucous membranes, and if you take anticoagulants, be careful with long-term use over large areas.

xylometazoline.tagline: Spray it and your nose clears within minutes — but the 3-day rule
xylometazoline.lead: It directly constricts the blood vessels in the nasal lining and clears the nose within minutes. Unlike oral decongestants it has little effect on blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure can use it briefly. The problem is that **using it for more than 3 days in a row causes rebound rhinitis — the nose gets more blocked when you stop**. Approved use: up to 3 times a day, not for 7 days in a row, and stop if it isn't better after 3 days.
stop: Using it for more than three days actually makes it more blocked — stop before then
Stop if you get frequent nosebleeds or sores inside the nose
Stop if your heart races
tips: For a blocked nose from a cold, using it at night for just 3 days and then stopping is the standard.
If your rhinitis comes back every season, a steroid nasal spray (prescription) is the answer — this one is for emergencies.

faq.q: How many days can I use it?
faq.a: Just 3 days. If you keep going longer, you get rebound rhinitis — the nose gets more blocked when you stop. The approved use is up to 3 times a day, not for 7 days in a row.

faq.q: My blood pressure is high — is it OK?
faq.a: Unlike oral decongestants it has little effect on blood pressure, so it can be used briefly. With high blood pressure or heart disease, talk to a pharmacist before using it, and don't use it if you have an enlarged prostate or angle-closure glaucoma (Korean leaflet).

xylometazoline.children: **Always check the strength.** 0.1% is for adults (12 and over), and **0.05% is for children from age 2 to under 12** (approved use — one spray at a time, 3 times a day, 8 hours apart). Don't spray the adult one in a child's nose.
